newsitem.title: SERBIA: FOCUS-Serbia takes pride in stability,vows reforms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Serbia takes pride in stability,vows reforms.

text.p: Serbia, with newly established price and currency stability, will begin to privatise its companies later this year after thorough preparations, Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic said.
A law allowing privatisation of almost 5,000 firms is expected to become effective late in October and Marjanovic said he hoped it would bring more efficiency and encourage growth.
In a written response to questions from Reuters, Marjanovic insisted there was no delay in implementing privatisation. "There is no delay, we really need several months to prepare," he said.
"Because of its complexity and political sensitiveness, we think that preparations for the implementation of the law should be adequate and comprehensive," he said.

Yugoslavia launched privatisation in the early 1990s but effects of the process were annulled in 1994 after a government decision which left the share of private shareholding capital at barely four percent.

Critics of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic at home and abroad have accused the his Socialists of foot-dragging on reform. Serbia is the dominant republic in what remains of the Yugoslav federation.
But Yugoslavia has overcome the hyperinflation of the early 1990s and stabilised the dinar exchange rate.
"Only price and currency stability creates an environment encouraging everyone to operate on market principles and be profit-oriented while increasing production and exports," said Marjanovic.
"Prices have been entirely stabilised so that their average monthly growth is below one percent," he said.
"The dinar exchange rate has also been stable with a very narrow spread between its official and market rates. Price and currency stability resulted in higher industry production and exports."

Retail prices fell 0.1 percent in June, after growing at a modest 0.1 or 0.2 percent monthly rate in April and May. The dinar is officially fixed at 3.3 to the German mark, while its market rate has been between 3.5 and 3.7 for months.

Marjanovic said Serbia was taking additional steps to strengthen stability while stimulating production and exports. "It is vital to maintain full fiscal discipline and balance public spending and public revenues, which eliminates the key cause of inflation and overall economic instability," he added.
He hoped privatisation would speed up rehabilitation of banks.

"Restructuring of companies, partially through their privatisation, will help speed up the bank overhaul programme. But...we expect banks to take steps on their own to downsize, restructure, increase efficiency, secure deposits, extend credits," Marjanovic said.
Yugoslav banks are struggling with low savings and deposits, reflecting a lack of faith in the financial system. Yugoslavs saved on the average just 11 dinars ($1.9) in 1996.
The crisis of confidence culminated after two pyramid savings schemes collapsed in 1993, the year when Yugoslavia faced hyper-inflation of 60 percent a day.

"The runaway inflation in the 1991-1993 period, before this government took office, devastated companies' and banks' accounts, made extended credits worthless and terribly intensified the problem of hard currency savings," Marjanovic said.
Yugoslavs have lost around $4 billion in hard currency deposits in 1991 after the government could not pay out savings invested in the economy.

Apart from frozen savings -- which the government recognises as a public debt and plans to issue bonds later this year to service -- Yugoslavia is also burdened with close to a $10 billion external debt and $7 billion in inter-company debt.
Independent economists forecast Yugoslavia's 1996 GDP at around $17 billion. Serbia accounts for 95 percent of it.

Last week, Yugoslavia reopened talks with its commercial creditors in London and asked for a 80 percent reduction of its $2.2 billion commercial debt. Creditors found the request unacceptable but agreed to resume talks by the end of July.
Serbia is seen in need of $1.5 billion to $2 billion a year to foster reforms and boost its idling industries.
Marjanovic said reforms would woo foreign interest.

"A healthy economic environment offered by an open market economy fostering competition would attract not only domestic investors but also woo foreign capital always in search for profitable projects and good business opportunities," he said. "Serbia and Yugoslavia offer such favourable conditions to everyone."
